bridges.statement: Taken together, Craig’s independent arguments make God’s existence the more plausible motion-level conclusion.
A transcendent personal necessary cause best explains why a contingent universe exists and began.
God grounds objective moral values that naturalistic evolution and convention cannot make binding.
The empty tomb, appearances, and origin of resurrection belief are best explained by divine action.
If a maximally great being is possible, modal necessity entails that God exists actually.
Immediate personal experience can rationally warrant belief in God apart from public argument.
Irreducible mentality and agency support an immaterial self and the coherence of an unembodied divine mind.
The expected evidence for an active, good creator is absent while natural accounts fit the observations, supporting God’s nonexistence.
An active revealed God should leave independently verifiable evidence in revelation, prayer, nature, and history.
Cosmology, evolution, and neuroscience provide plausible natural accounts without a supernatural posit.
Hiddenness and extensive apparently needless suffering conflict with an available and morally good God.
Late, disputed, and internally problematic resurrection sources do not establish a divine miracle.
Human biological and social development can yield shared moral codes without divine grounding.
Brain dependence of consciousness supports a material account rather than an immortal immaterial soul.

sections.title: Modal Possibility and Contingent Explanation
sections.rationale: Craig's ontological and contingency routes receive Stenger's premise challenge and Craig's distinct coherence and explanatory replies.

sections.title: Cosmic Origin, Causation, and Temporal Boundaries
sections.rationale: The speakers contest causal premises, zero energy, quantum origins, no-boundary models, past limits, and timeless simultaneous causation.

sections.title: Naturalistic Explanatory Reach: Design, Mind, and Time
sections.rationale: Evolutionary complexity, mind-brain dependence, physical time, materialist data, and epistemic reliability test the reach of natural explanation.

sections.title: Morality, Hiddenness, and the Evidential Force of Evil
sections.rationale: Objective moral grounding, natural moral development, nonbelief, extensive suffering, and possible divine reasons form one evaluative burden cluster.

sections.title: Resurrection Evidence and Historical Warrant
sections.rationale: Competing claims about source plurality, empty-tomb tradition, appearances, martyrdom, alternatives, and scholarly support drive the historical exchange.

sections.title: Public Evidence, Revelation, and Prayer
sections.rationale: Stenger's testable-evidence program focuses on revelation and prayer, while Craig answers the expectation premise and closes cumulatively.

sections.title: Personal Experience and Competing Proof Burdens
sections.rationale: Craig's immediate experiential warrant meets Stenger's verification demand and his claim that extraordinary supernatural conclusions bear the heavier burden.
